newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Hope for S.African economy in 1998 - fund manager.
newsitem.headline: Hope for S.African economy in 1998 - fund manager.

text.p: South Africa could lay the foundations next year for economic growth in 1998 if it takes prudent steps now including the use of privatisation proceeds to retire debt, the Board of Executors (BOE) said on Thursday.
"It is clear that 1997 will be a tough year for the South African economy," BOE chief economist Rob Lee said in his December investment outlook.

"Economic growth will decline and inflation will be higher. However, the foundations for a subsequent long-term improvement in economic performance could be laid, providing there is sufficient progress in structural reform."

Lee listed as conditions for an eventual turnaround a stronger international economy, relaxation of exchange controls, Reserve Bank withdrawal from the forward cover market and use of the IMF's offer of a $2.0 billion stand-by facility.
Labour unions would have to contribute by holding wage increases below the recently accelerated inflation rate.

In addition, Lee said, the current 14 percent value added tax rate should be increased, government consumption expenditure should be curbed and the proceeds of significant privatisation should largely be used to pay off state debts.
"Given the critical importance of restoring health to government finances, we would urge that most if not all of privatisation proceeds should be used to retire debt.

"Given these conditions, the outlook from 1998 onwards would be for accelerating economic growth, falling inflation and interest rates , a more stable currency - probably lower than at present - and foreign capital inflows financing a sustainable level of current account deficits.
"Investment strategies should remain cautious, but be ready to be aggressively positive if and when the above conditions are seen to be unfolding," he said.
Lee identified five "silver linings" to the generally dark economic outlook, including:
- A clear commitment by the ruling African National Congress to good governance.
- A favourable international economic climate with a prospect of modestly improved commodity prices.
- A renewal of tough monetary policy amid signs of a reduction in the deficit on the current account of the balance of payments, a reduction in domestic spending growth and falling credit growth.
- Favourable fiscal developments including improved tax collection and an increase in effective government spending on infrastructure.
- Accelerated government implementation of its economic reform programme including concrete moves towards privatisation.
